cards.a: To show how much product forms without the enzyme, so that background change can be subtracted.
options: To provide extra substrate that can be added later if needed
To measure the maximum reaction rate the enzyme can reach
To calibrate the wavelength setting used by the spectrophotometer
To show how much change occurs without enzyme, so background can be subtracted
cards.explanation: Some substrates break down slowly on their own, and the no enzyme control tells you how much of the signal to credit to the enzyme rather than to spontaneous change. The maximum rate is measured in a tube with enzyme at optimal conditions, not in one without it. A control is not a reagent reservoir, and wavelength selection is based on the product's absorbance spectrum.

cards.q: Why are all tubes in a pH series kept in the same 37 C water bath?
cards.a: To hold temperature constant so that any difference in rate can be attributed to pH.
options: To speed up every reaction so that the lab session finishes on time
To keep the buffer solutions from evaporating during the run
To ensure the enzyme denatures at the same rate in every tube
To hold temperature constant so that differences in rate can be attributed to pH
cards.explanation: Controlling every variable except the one under study is what lets you interpret the result, since a tube that was both warmer and more acidic would give an uninterpretable answer. Saving time is a side benefit, not the design reason. Evaporation is minor over a short assay, and you want to avoid denaturation in a pH experiment, not standardize it.

cards.q: A student assays a human enzyme and records rates of 0.02, 0.09, 0.21, 0.08, and 0.01 absorbance units per minute at 5, 20, 37, 50, and 70 C. What is the optimum temperature?
cards.explanation: The highest rate, 0.21 per minute, occurs at 37 C, which matches the body temperature this enzyme evolved to work at. The rate at 20 C is still climbing toward the peak. Rates at 50 and 70 C are low because the enzyme is denaturing, so higher temperature does not keep improving performance.

cards.q: A pH series gives rates of 0.01, 0.05, 0.22, 0.19, and 0.03 absorbance units per minute at pH 3, 5, 7, 8, and 11. What is the optimum pH for this enzyme?
cards.a: pH 7.
options: pH 5
pH 3
pH 11
pH 7
cards.explanation: The peak rate of 0.22 per minute falls at pH 7, with pH 8 close behind on the shoulder of the curve. Rates at pH 5 and pH 3 are low because the enzyme is progressively denatured on the acid side. pH 11 gives the near zero activity expected when strong alkali has unfolded the protein.

cards.q: Two tubes are plotted as absorbance against time. Tube A gives a steeper line than tube B. What does that tell you?
cards.a: The enzyme in tube A is producing product faster.
options: Tube A started with more product already present
Tube A contains a larger volume of solution
Tube A was read at a longer wavelength
The enzyme in tube A is producing product faster
cards.explanation: Slope is change in absorbance over change in time, which is exactly the definition of reaction rate, so a steeper line means faster product formation. Starting product would raise the intercept of the line rather than tilt it. Volume differences are eliminated by using matched cuvettes and standard volumes, and the wavelength is held constant for all tubes in an assay.

cards.q: A student forgets to blank the spectrophotometer and instead zeroes it on air. Predict the effect on the recorded absorbance values and on the calculated rate.
cards.a: All absorbance readings are shifted upward, but the calculated rate from the slope is largely unaffected.
options: All readings are shifted upward, but the rate calculated from the slope is largely unaffected
All readings are shifted upward, and the calculated rate is proportionally too high
All readings are shifted downward, and the calculated rate is too low
Readings are unaffected, since the blank matters only for color intensity
cards.explanation: A missing blank adds a constant offset from the buffer and cuvette to every reading, and a constant added to all points raises the line without changing its slope, so the rate survives even though the individual values are wrong. Treating the error as proportional confuses an additive offset with a multiplicative one. Adding the solution's own absorbance raises rather than lowers readings, and blanking affects the numbers regardless of how intense the color is.

cards.q: Predict the shape of the activity curve for a human enzyme as temperature rises from 0 C through 60 C.
cards.a: A gradual rise to a peak near 37 C followed by a steep drop as the enzyme denatures.
options: A gradual rise to a peak near 37 C, then a steep drop as denaturation sets in
A steady rise all the way to 60 C
A symmetric bell with equally gradual rise and fall on both sides of 37 C
A flat line, since human enzymes are buffered against temperature change
cards.explanation: Below the optimum, rate climbs gradually as molecular motion increases, but above it the fold comes apart quickly and aggregation makes the loss abrupt and largely irreversible, so the curve is lopsided. A steady rise ignores denaturation entirely. A symmetric bell would imply the fall is as gentle as the rise, and a flat line would mean temperature does not matter, which is contradicted by any assay you run.

cards.q: With substrate at a saturating concentration, a student doubles the amount of enzyme added to the tube. Predict the slope of the absorbance versus time line.
cards.a: About twice as steep.
options: Unchanged, because substrate is saturating
About twice as steep
About half as steep, because the enzyme molecules compete
Steeper at first and then flat within seconds
cards.explanation: Vmax is proportional to the number of active sites, so twice the enzyme converts substrate about twice as fast and the line rises twice as quickly. Saturating substrate means the enzyme is the limiting factor, which is exactly why adding enzyme helps here. Enzyme molecules do not interfere with each other, and with substrate in excess the reaction does not exhaust its supply within seconds.

cards.q: A lab group assays pepsin and trypsin across pH 1 to 10 and finds peak activity for pepsin near pH 2 and for trypsin near pH 8. What accounts for the difference?
cards.a: Each enzyme's active site holds its working shape at the pH of the compartment where it normally acts, the stomach for pepsin and the small intestine for trypsin.
options: Trypsin is the stronger enzyme, so it can work across a much wider range of pH values
Each enzyme's active site keeps its shape only near the pH of the compartment where it normally works
Pepsin is denatured at pH 2, so its apparent peak reflects nonenzymatic breakdown of the substrate
The buffers used at low pH absorb more light on their own, which artificially raises the pepsin reading
cards.explanation: Optimum pH is a property of the enzyme's own side chain charges, and each digestive enzyme is built to fold correctly in the compartment where it is secreted, which is why pepsin fails once it reaches the alkaline intestine. Strength is not a meaningful comparison between enzymes with different substrates. Pepsin is stable and active at pH 2, not denatured by it, and a properly blanked assay corrects for the absorbance of the buffer itself.

cards.q: A student's progress curve rises steeply for the first minute and then flattens, and she concludes the enzyme denatured. What is the more likely explanation, and how should the rate be reported?
cards.a: Substrate was used up, and the rate should be taken from the initial linear part of the curve.
options: The enzyme denatured, so the rate should be taken from the flat portion of the curve
The spectrophotometer drifted, so the whole run must be discarded
Substrate ran out, and the rate should be taken from the initial linear portion of the curve
Product inhibited the enzyme, so the rate should be averaged over the entire run
cards.explanation: A curve that flattens while conditions are held constant almost always means the substrate is exhausted, which is why initial velocity, measured while substrate is still plentiful, is the standard reported value. Denaturation would show as a decline over a series of temperature conditions rather than a plateau in a single tube at 37 C. Instrument drift would produce erratic or sloping baselines rather than a clean plateau, and averaging over a run that includes the plateau systematically underestimates the true rate.

cards.q: One enzyme sample is held at 5 C and another at 80 C, then both are returned to 37 C and assayed. The chilled sample works normally and the heated one shows no activity. What does this pair of results demonstrate?
cards.a: Cold slows the enzyme reversibly, while high heat denatures it irreversibly.
options: Cold slows the enzyme reversibly, while high heat denatures it irreversibly
Both treatments denature the enzyme, but cold denaturation is slower to appear
The enzyme has two optima, one near 5 C and one near 37 C
Heat destroys the substrate rather than the enzyme, so no product can form
cards.explanation: The chilled enzyme simply lacked kinetic energy and recovers as soon as it is warmed, whereas the heated one unfolded and its exposed hydrophobic regions aggregated, so warming it back to 37 C cannot restore the fold. Cold does not denature the enzyme in this range, which is exactly why the chilled sample recovers. A single enzyme has one optimum, and the substrate was added fresh to both tubes after the temperature treatment.

cards.q: Tube A shows an absorbance change of 0.45 over 3 minutes and tube B shows 0.30 over 5 minutes. Calculate each rate and state which enzyme sample is more active.
cards.a: Tube A is 0.15 per minute and tube B is 0.06 per minute, so tube A is more active.
options: Tube A is 0.15 per minute and tube B is 0.06 per minute, so tube B is more active
Tube B is more active, because its total absorbance change was measured over a longer time
Both are equally active, because absorbance eventually reaches the same value
Tube A is 0.15 per minute and tube B is 0.06 per minute, so tube A is more active
cards.explanation: Dividing each absorbance change by its own time gives 0.45 divided by 3, or 0.15 per minute, and 0.30 divided by 5, or 0.06 per minute, so tube A works more than twice as fast. Comparing raw absorbance changes without dividing by time is the usual error and would wrongly favor whichever tube ran longer. Reaching a similar endpoint eventually says nothing about rate, which is the quantity enzyme activity is defined by.
